what_it_does: Running a large language model locally on an edge device (a laptop, a small server at a hospital reception desk, etc.) is bottlenecked by how fast data can travel from the main memory chips (DRAM — the storage that holds the model's billions of numbers) to the processor. H2-LLM proposes a chip architecture that uses hybrid bonding — a manufacturing technique that stacks a high-compute logic die face-to-face directly on top of DRAM dies with dense microscopic copper connections — to place far more arithmetic capacity right next to the memory, dramatically reducing the distance data must travel. Because generating tokens (the decoding phase) and processing the input prompt (the prefill phase) have different computational needs, the system maps each operation to the most suitable compute resources on the stacked die. A design-space search tool automatically finds the best balance between compute tiles and memory bandwidth for a given model and workload. This is from the abstract only.
